title: Delhi High Court Allows Sonam Wangchuk's Transfer to Medanta Hospital
excerpt: A Division Bench overturned a single-judge order that had refused the climate activist's transfer from Safdarjung Hospital, with government raising no objection to the move.
body:
• Delhi HC Division Bench led by Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya ordered Wangchuk's transfer from Safdarjung Hospital to Medanta Hospital in Gurugram.
  • The ruling overturns a July 19 single-judge order by Justice Mini Pushkarna that had declined to grant the transfer, saying the government's decision to hospitalise Wangchuk was not arbitrary.
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, representing the government, expressed no objection to the move but insisted on strict medical supervision at Medanta.
  • Wangchuk, 59, has been on an indefinite hunger strike since June 28 in solidarity with student protests demanding accountability for the NEET-UG paper leak.

The Delhi High Court on Tuesday ordered the transfer of climate activist and education reformer Sonam Wangchuk from Safdarjung Hospital to Medanta Hospital in Gurugram, ending a legal tussle over his medical care that had played out across two benches in three days.

A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia allowed the transfer after reviewing Wangchuk's medical records and consulting doctors from AIIMS, Safdarjung Hospital, and the activist's own medical team. All sides reached a consensus that Wangchuk required constant medical supervision — a condition that could be met at Medanta, the hospital his family had requested.

How the Legal Battle Unfolded

Wangchuk, 59, began his indefinite hunger strike at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on June 28 in solidarity with the youth-led "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which is demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG examination paper leak that affected millions of students. By July 18 — the 21st day of his fast — Delhi Police removed him from the protest site and shifted him to Safdarjung Hospital, citing concerns over his deteriorating health.

His wife, Dr. Gitanjali Angmo, immediately moved the High Court, alleging that his continued hospitalisation amounted to "illegal detention" and that medical intervention was being used as a pretext to keep him from the protest site. She accused the hospital of lacking transparency in sharing medical records and challenged the authority under which he had been forcibly removed.

"His confinement is being affected purely in the garb and under the pretext of 'medical intervention', without any formal legal order, as a device to remove him from, and prevent his return to, the site of his peaceful protest."

— Gitanjali Angmo, in her petition to Delhi High Court

On July 19, Justice Mini Pushkarna declined to grant interim relief, ruling that the government's decision to hospitalise Wangchuk was not arbitrary given his worsening medical parameters — blood sugar, sodium, and potassium levels had reportedly fallen below safe limits. Angmo appealed the order the same day, arguing it violated Wangchuk's bodily autonomy and his right under Article 21 of the Constitution to choose his own medical care.

Division Bench Reverses Course

Senior Advocate Akhil Sibal, representing Angmo before the Division Bench, pointed to Wangchuk's stable vital signs and alleged that his stay at Safdarjung was marked by police surveillance and restricted communication. The appeal further noted that independent tests had recorded Wangchuk's potassium levels at 3.6 and 3.76 — within normal range — contradicting the hospital's earlier claim that levels had dropped to a dangerous 2.9.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the government, did not oppose the transfer but stressed that Wangchuk must remain under strict medical supervision at Medanta until doctors there cleared him. The bench accepted this condition.

A Protest That Has Tested the Government

Wangchuk's fast — now in its 24th day — has become a focal point of the broader student-led campaign that Reuters has described as "a rare public challenge" to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government. The Cockroach Janta Party, a satirical protest group formed by Indian youth outraged by exam irregularities, has drawn support across the country.

On Monday, Union Minister JP Nadda held talks with CJP representatives, who submitted a list of demands including accountability for the paper leak. Hours later, Wangchuk issued a handwritten note through his wife, vowing to continue his fast "until the youth leaders are allowed to meet the parliamentarians at Sansad Bhawan or I am allowed to meet them here at the hospital."

What Happens Next

Wangchuk's transfer to Medanta is expected to be carried out under the conditions set by the court. His medical team will take over his care, though the government retains its interest in ensuring he receives continuous monitoring. The broader legal proceedings — including questions about the legality of his removal from Jantar Mantar and the scope of the July 16 court order that police relied upon — remain pending before the High Court.

For the Indian diaspora watching the exam-reform protests with growing interest, the court's decision offers a measure of relief. Wangchuk, best known internationally for his ice stupa innovation and the inspiration behind the film 3 Idiots, has become the movement's most recognizable figure. Whether the government engages meaningfully with the students' demands may determine how much longer his fast continues.
